candidate_relations.reason: Hip weakness and iliopsoas edema localize symptoms but do not explain the systemic inflammatory rise.
Left insertional tendinopathy was visible on MRI as a focal finding within a broader bilateral inflammatory process.
No pulmonary, nodal, calcium, or biopsy evidence supported sarcoidosis.
No synovitis or small-joint arthritis was described despite escalating girdle-region inflammation.
Fluid-responsive hypotension and pre-renal kidney injury indicate dehydration but not the persistent hip inflammatory syndrome.
Repeated infection investigations were unrevealing and symptoms persisted without an identified source.
Giant cell arteritis is associated with PMR, but no headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptom was reported.
Urgent lumbar MRI showed no epidural collection.
He arrived hypotensive, and hypertension cannot account for progressive painful proximal weakness.
Lumbar MRI found neither canal compression nor hematoma.
Insertional iliopsoas abnormality can contribute to hip pain but does not encompass bilateral muscle edema and raised ESR/CRP.
There was no sacroiliitis, inflammatory back pain, or spinal imaging evidence of spondyloarthritis.
Colchicine failed and no crystal-bearing aspirate or typical gouty joint was obtained.
The examination and imaging lacked the persistent polyarticular synovitis required for rheumatoid arthritis.
Creatine kinase was normal, while the edema centered on bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas structures.
Six-month weight loss and anorexia suggest malnutrition but do not cause the high inflammatory markers and MRI enhancement.
Alzheimer dementia was established history and is unrelated to the new painful proximal motor decline.
MRI explicitly found muscle edema and tendinopathy without reporting an iliopsoas bursal collection.
Presumed crystal arthropathy did not improve with colchicine and aspiration yielded no diagnostic crystals.
Only a small effusion was seen, with bilateral periarticular muscle changes and no cultured joint pathogen.

case_quality_flags: The excerpt lacks shoulder-girdle symptoms and a documented rapid glucocorticoid response, making the PMR reference less directly supported than usual.
